When Does Crime Enter House Prices?

When Does Crime Enter House Prices? Evidence from Chicago

Nency Dhameja

Job Market Paper  ·  __DATE__

Paper (PDF)Online Appendix
Question

__Q__

Main finding
I find that closing-price discounts appear across multiple exposure windows for four offenses. Homicide has the largest estimated discount, about 3 percent per victim; burglary, narcotics, and vandalism reduce prices by 0.24, 0.29, and 0.17 percent per incident. Disorderly conduct and sex offenses are significant only at one long-horizon window, while theft, motor-vehicle theft, assault, and robbery have no detectable discount.
Data

Offense categories
22
Years
2007–2025

I link 530,395 single-family, condominium, and residential-income transactions on 337,461 properties from the Chicago Multiple Listing Service, spanning 2007 to 2025, to 5.59 million geocoded crime incidents, analyzing twenty-two offense categories.

Identification
Figure 2. The near–far design.

I compare the same property across sales (parcel fixed effects), relative to other sales in its census tract in the same month (tract-by-month fixed effects).

Additionally, I contrast crime within 0.05 miles of the property (roughly the same block) with crime in a comparison ring 0.20–0.30 miles away.

I apply this design to all twenty-two offenses and assess its validity using post-sale crime placebos, since subsequent incidents cannot causally affect a price already set.

Results

Each estimate is the percent change in the sale price per nearby incident (withdrawal: percentage points). The window is how many months of crime before the sale are counted.

Median window: the median of the exposure windows with a discount significant at 5 percent (lower median if even); twelve months for offenses with none.

Why only some offenses are priced

How buyers use crime information

Price effects are hyperlocal, but crime’s predictive content extends farther: crime a few blocks away predicts future crime near the property for every offense at twelve months, yet it has no statistically significant price effect.

Observability

For some offenses, incidents at a home’s frontage lower prices, while those inside the dwelling have no statistically significant price effect.

Real estate agents

Holding total experience constant, asking-price declines are larger for several offenses (robbery, fraud, and domestic and non-domestic assault) when listing agents have more prior listings in the tract.
The transaction

Asking prices

Domestic assault lowers asking prices among homes that sell (−0.33 percent at twelve months, s.e. 0.10; Figure 4, panel A), the only asking-price response that is robust across fixed-effects specifications.

Sale-to-list ratio

Narcotics instead lowers the sale-to-list ratio under both fixed-effects specifications (−0.16 percent at ten months, s.e. 0.06; Online Appendix Figure OF3). Because its asking price does not change, the discount appears after listing, consistent with buyers learning of these incidents during their search and negotiating lower prices.

Weapons violations and withdrawals

The clearest friction is for weapons violations, which raise the probability that a listing is withdrawn, leaving the market without a sale (0.63 percentage points at six months, s.e. 0.18), and the probability that a home comes back on the market after an earlier listing failed to sell (0.36 at eight months, s.e. 0.16; Online Appendix E.1), under both specifications (Online Appendix Figures OF6 and OF7).

PIN: parcel and tract × month fixed effects; PIN×era: parcel-by-era and tract × month fixed effects. Placebo: crime after the transaction. Reverse Causality and Mean ReversionFigure 6 · Figure A9 · Figure A11 · Table A4

For the four priced offenses, the placebo estimates are insignificant in almost all specifications: across 63 specifications per offense, crime after the sale is significant in none for homicide or vandalism, one for narcotics, and four for burglary (bottom panels of Figure 6 and Figures A9–A11).

Main vs. post-sale placebo, every window
Prior Neighborhood and Housing-Market ConditionsTable A22

Point estimates and standard errors change little (Appendix Table A22), and all four discounts remain significant at the five-percent level when all ten controls are included.

Baseline vs. all ten predetermined controls, every window
Cross-Crime ConfoundingTable OA27 · Table A4

A discount attributed to one offense could reflect another offense that occurs nearby. Entering all twenty-two offenses’ near–far terms jointly at a common twelve-month window leaves their estimates nearly unchanged (Online Appendix Table OA27; separate estimates in Appendix Table A4).

Separate vs. all twenty-two offenses entered jointly, common twelve-month window
Sample SelectionTable OA18 · Table A23

First, nearby crime barely changes whether a parcel sells. In an annual panel of all Chicago dwelling parcels, with parcel and tract-by-year fixed effects and crime measured in the previous year, burglary is the only priced offense with a statistically significant effect on the probability that a parcel sells, 0.05 percentage points (s.e. 0.01) against a base rate of 3.8 percent (Table OA18).

Third test: hedonic regression on all sales (including homes that sell once) vs. repeat sales, each offense at its median window
Selection into Zero ExposureTable A7

For narcotics and vandalism, the coefficient on the indicator is not statistically significant once the baseline fixed effects are included. For burglary, the coefficient is significant even with parcel fixed effects (−0.98, s.e. 0.32): sales with no nearby burglary sell for about one percent less than the relationship among exposed sales predicts.

Zero-exposure indicator as fixed effects are added, each offense at its median window
Functional FormTable OA26 · Table OA7

Homicide’s estimated discount remains significant under all three at its median window.

Raw count vs. presence indicator vs. inverse hyperbolic sine, every window
Spatial Standard ErrorsTable OA23

Conley standard errors that allow correlation across tract boundaries, with cutoffs of 0.5 and 1.0 km (Conley 1999), give similar inference: homicide, burglary, and vandalism remain significant at five percent under both cutoffs, and narcotics at five percent at 0.5 km and ten percent at 1.0 km (Table OA23). Clustering instead by the 77 community areas, a much coarser unit, leaves homicide and burglary significant at five percent and vandalism at ten percent, while narcotics is not significant at ten percent (p = 0.12).

Priced offenses at their median windows: 95% intervals under each standard error
Specification curves: sale pricesFigure 6 · Figure A9 · Figure A11 · Figure A12 · Figure A8 · Figure OF10 · Figure OF13

The discount is significant at five percent in 33 of 63 specifications for vandalism, 29 for narcotics, 29 for burglary, and 15 for homicide, whose point estimates range from about −3.6 percent to about zero with wide intervals.

How to read the curves

Each curve sorts the near–far discount across specifications that vary the exposure window, the fixed effects, the comparison ring, the functional form, and the predetermined controls (Section __SCSEC__).
